hero.description: Wat Si Saket is the old-city temple to slow down for: its cloister, thousands of Buddha images and survival through the destruction of Vientiane in 1828 give the site a density that is easy to miss from the street.

Walk the cloister before the main hall
Look closely at the Buddha niches
Pair the visit with Haw Phra Kaew opposite
hero.rhythmNote: This is a detail-first temple. Give the cloister more attention than the checklist photo and let the repetition of small Buddha images set the pace.

chapters.label: THE SURVIVOR
chapters.title: One temple carries an unusual amount of old Vientiane
chapters.body: Wat Si Saket was built in 1818 under King Anouvong and is noted by Tourism Laos as the only ancient temple to remain intact after the destruction of Vientiane in 1828. That survival makes the monastery more than another temple stop: its architecture and enclosed courtyard preserve a continuity that much of the capital lost.

chapters.label: THE CLOISTER
chapters.title: Repetition is the experience
chapters.body: The courtyard walls and niches hold thousands of Buddha images in different scales. Do not try to count or isolate a single masterpiece. Walk the cloister slowly and let the accumulation do the work; the visual rhythm is what makes Si Saket distinct from the larger golden monuments elsewhere in the city.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: If you only have time for one old-city temple interior, Si Saket gives the strongest sense of historical continuity.

chapters.label: PAIRING
chapters.title: Cross the road for the complementary museum
chapters.body: Haw Phra Kaew sits almost opposite and tells a different story: a former royal temple turned museum. Visiting the two together gives you architecture, devotional history and collected Buddhist art without adding transport.

beforeYouLeave.title: Keep the morning compact
beforeYouLeave.body: Si Saket, Haw Phra Kaew and nearby central streets can form one walkable block before the day becomes hotter. Save Patuxai and That Luang for the inland leg.

note.label: BEST USE
note.text: This is one of Vientiane’s cleanest low-transport cultural pairings.

items.label: Time needed
items.detail: The footprint is small, but the cloister rewards a slower visit.

items.label: Getting there
items.detail: Walkable from many central hotels and directly paired with Haw Phra Kaew.

items.label: Best time
items.detail: Cooler conditions suit the courtyard and leave the rest of the day open for outer landmarks.

items.label: Entry
items.detail: Tourism Laos currently lists an admission fee and split opening hours around midday; reconfirm locally.

faq.question: Why is Wat Si Saket important?
faq.answer: It was built in 1818 and is noted as the only ancient Vientiane temple to remain intact after the city’s destruction in 1828.

faq.question: What is special about the Buddha images?
faq.answer: The cloister and courtyard walls contain thousands of Buddha images and small niches, creating the temple’s distinctive visual rhythm.

faq.question: How long should I allow?
faq.answer: About 45 to 75 minutes is comfortable if you want to walk the cloister rather than rush through the compound.

faq.question: What should I visit next?
faq.answer: Haw Phra Kaew is directly opposite and is the natural companion visit.

faq.question: Is there an entrance fee?
faq.answer: Yes. Tourism Laos currently lists paid admission; confirm the current price and hours at the site.
